diagnostics.message:
[final-deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-effort-high-run1]
aws_lambda_function.pool is created with a vpc_config block whenever var.config.lambda.subnet_ids is non-empty, but it only references aws_iam_role.pool — nothing orders aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.pool_vpc_execution_role (gated by the exact same subnet_ids condition) before the function. Lambda must be able to call ec2:CreateNetworkInterface to attach ENIs at creation time, so without the AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole policy already attached the apply fails with "The provided execution role does not have permissions to call CreateNetworkInterface on EC2". Add depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.pool_vpc_execution_role] to aws_lambda_function.pool.

----------------------------------------

[final-deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-effort-high-run2]
aws_lambda_function.pool is provisioned with a vpc_config (when var.config.lambda.subnet_ids/security_group_ids are set), so Lambda attaches the function to the VPC using the execution role. It only references aws_iam_role.pool.arn; the AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole policy is attached separately by aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.pool_vpc_execution_role, which the function does not depend on. Because IAM policy attachment is eventually consistent, function creation races the attachment and can fail with "The provided execution role does not have permissions to call CreateNetworkInterface on EC2". The Lambda should be ordered after the VPC execution role attachment (e.g. depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.pool_vpc_execution_role]). No clean attribute-level data reference exists for the attachment, so a bare depends_on is appropriate.

----------------------------------------

[final-deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-effort-high-run3]
aws_lambda_function.pool is created with a vpc_config block (when var.config.lambda.subnet_ids/security_group_ids are set), but it has no dependency on aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.pool_vpc_execution_role, which attaches AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole to its execution role. Both are gated on the same subnet_ids condition and both depend only on aws_iam_role.pool, so they are created concurrently. Lambda needs ec2:CreateNetworkInterface/DescribeNetworkInterfaces on the execution role while creating the function's VPC networking; without the attachment first, creation intermittently fails with "The provided execution role does not have permissions to call CreateNetworkInterface on EC2". The function should be created after the VPC access policy attachment.

[final-deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-effort-high-run1]
All of aws_lambda_function.pool's core runtime permissions (SSM config/token parameters, EC2 runner lifecycle, tagging) live in the inline policy aws_iam_role_policy.pool, which the function does not depend on — it only references aws_iam_role.pool.arn. Terraform will therefore happily finish creating the pool Lambda (and let the scheduler or a manual invoke hit it) before the role's policy exists, producing AccessDenied errors on the first invocations. The aws_lambda_function documentation's "ensure IAM role and log group are ready" example handles exactly this with an explicit depends_on; aws_lambda_function.pool should depend on aws_iam_role_policy.pool.

----------------------------------------

[final-deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-effort-high-run3]
aws_lambda_function.pool and aws_iam_role_policy.pool (the function's main execution policy: SSM parameter access, EC2/ASG calls, KMS, iam:PassRole) only share aws_iam_role.pool as a dependency, so Terraform creates the function and the role policy in parallel. Nothing prevents the function from becoming live — and being invoked by aws_scheduler_schedule.pool, which is created enabled — before the policy has been attached to its execution role, producing AccessDenied failures on the first scheduled run. The function should depend on the policy that grants its runtime permissions.

[final-deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-effort-high-run1]
aws_scheduler_schedule.pool points target.role_arn at aws_iam_role.scheduler.arn and therefore waits for the role, but the lambda:InvokeFunction permission the target actually needs is in the separate inline policy aws_iam_role_policy.scheduler, which no edge orders before the schedule. Because the schedule uses flexible_time_window mode = "OFF" (an exact, immediately-active schedule_expression), the first fire can happen while the execution role still has no invoke permission, and the pool is never resized until the next scheduled run. Add depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.scheduler] to aws_scheduler_schedule.pool.

----------------------------------------

[final-deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-effort-high-run2]
aws_scheduler_schedule.pool triggers aws_lambda_function.pool using aws_iam_role.scheduler, but it only references the role's ARN. The permission that actually lets that role invoke the Lambda (lambda:InvokeFunction) lives in aws_iam_role_policy.scheduler, a sibling resource attached in parallel. Because IAM inline policies are eventually consistent, Terraform can create the schedule before the role is authorized, so the schedule's first invocation can fail with an authorization error. The schedule should depend on aws_iam_role_policy.scheduler (e.g. depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.scheduler]); there is no attribute on the schedule that can carry this reference.

----------------------------------------

[final-deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-effort-high-run3]
aws_scheduler_schedule.pool targets aws_lambda_function.pool with role_arn = aws_iam_role.scheduler.arn, but it does not depend on aws_iam_role_policy.scheduler, the inline policy that actually grants the scheduler role lambda:InvokeFunction. The policy is only ordered after data.aws_iam_policy_document.scheduler (which needs the function ARN), so it can be created after the schedule. Since aws_scheduler_schedule resources are created ENABLED and can fire immediately, the first invocation can fail with AccessDeniedException because the assumed role has no permission to invoke the target. The schedule should be created after the role policy that gives it invoke permission.
